fieldData.name: Fixing Lead Quality: Agency Leads, Sales Rejections and the Qualification Handoff
fieldData.meta-title: Fixing Lead Quality: Agency Leads and the Handoff
fieldData.meta-description: Why sales rejects agency leads: where the definition breaks, the nine field handover record, the two way SLA, and the 50 lead audit that settles the argument.
fieldData.post-summary: An operational fix for agency lead quality disputes, written for the client side of the contract: why rejection is usually a definition problem, the three places the definition breaks, the nine field handover record, the two way qualification SLA with a consequence clause, how to audit the last fifty rejected leads into four countable buckets, and when the agency is right and sales is wrong.
fieldData.post-body:
Arguments about lead quality, agency performance and whose fault it is are almost always a definition problem rather than a quality problem. The agency is delivering against the criteria in the contract, sales is rejecting against criteria that were never written down, and both sides are correct. Until one written definition governs what counts as qualified, what gets handed over, and how fast it is worked, the argument repeats every quarter.

This is written for the person on the client side of that contract: the revenue leader paying an agency for leads their own sales team keeps rejecting. The agency lead handoff is the mechanism, and the fix is operational and yours to make, because the definition lives in your CRM and your comp plan, not in the agency's. The internal version of this seam, between marketing and sales inside one company, is covered in our piece on the sales and marketing handoff. This one is about the seam that crosses a contract, which is harder because one side bills for volume.

The Short Answer: Lead Quality, Agency Criteria and Who Owns the Gap

Every MQL rejected by sales is either a record that genuinely misses the written criteria or a record that misses criteria nobody wrote down, and those two look identical in a dashboard. Three symptoms tell you it is definitional rather than real. Rejection reasons are inconsistent between reps. Nobody can produce the written criteria without opening the contract. And the agency's monthly report and your CRM disagree on how many leads were delivered. Any one of those means the two sides are measuring different objects.

The structural reason is that lead count is the only thing in the relationship that is cleanly countable. An agency can be held to volume because volume is unambiguous. Qualification is a judgement, so it gets deferred to a scoring threshold nobody can explain, and a threshold is not a definition. Forrester's analysis of the end of MQLs notes that inquiry to closed won conversion in a lead centric process typically runs under 1 percent, which tells you how little a lead count predicts on its own.

That does not make the agency blameless. It makes the contract the first place to look, before anyone reviews a single record. We make the broader case in lead quality versus quantity in B2B; this page is the operational fix for the specific case where money is changing hands over the number.

The Three Places the Definition Breaks

The lead qualification criteria agency contracts carry are usually the first thing to read, and they break in three predictable places.

1. The ICP is described, not specified. The contract says mid-market B2B SaaS in North America. That is a description. A specification names the fields, the permitted values and the source of truth: employee count from which provider, industry from which taxonomy, region from billing address or from the contact's own location. Without that, the agency fills the gap with its own reasonable reading and the records look wrong to your team for reasons neither side can articulate.

2. Qualification conflates fit with readiness. Fit is whether this company could ever buy. Readiness is whether they are in the market now. An agency can reliably deliver fit, because fit is observable from firmographics. Readiness depends on signals that mostly live in your product and your CRM, which the agency cannot see. A contract that pays for qualified leads without separating the two is asking for something the agency structurally cannot supply. Our guide to intent data and buying signals covers where readiness signals actually come from.

3. Timing is unowned. A lead handed over on Friday and first touched on Wednesday is a different asset from the same lead touched in an hour. The Harvard Business Review audit of 2,241 US companies found that firms responding to an online lead within an hour were nearly seven times more likely to qualify it, and that 23 percent never responded at all. When nobody owns response time, decay gets recorded as poor lead quality, and the agency is blamed for a delay on your side.

What Should Be Handed Over With Every Lead

A name and an email is not a handover, it is a row. The minimum record that prevents the argument has nine fields, and you can copy this list into the contract as an appendix: company identifier, the firmographic fields the ICP specifies with the provider named, the contact and their buying role, the stated problem in the prospect's own words, the source and campaign, the consent record with its timestamp and wording, what the prospect was told would happen next, the agency's own qualification note, and a handover timestamp.

The two fields that get skipped are the two that matter most. What the prospect was told would happen next determines whether your rep's opening line matches the prospect's expectation; when it does not, the call fails for reasons unrelated to fit. The agency's qualification note is the audit trail: one sentence on why this record met the criteria. Without it you cannot distinguish a judgement you disagree with from no judgement at all.

Require the record in one structured format written directly to your CRM, not a spreadsheet emailed monthly. A spreadsheet guarantees the reconciliation problem, because both sides then maintain their own count and neither can be audited against the other.

The Qualification SLA That Prevents the Argument

Make it two way, in writing, before the first lead. The agency commits to the specification, the payload and a stated accuracy bar: the share of delivered records that match the ICP fields on inspection. You commit to a response window, a rejection window, and a mandatory structured rejection reason from a fixed list.

The clause that makes it real is the consequence clause. A target without a consequence is a preference. Name what happens when either side misses: records outside the specification are replaced rather than counted, and records not touched inside the response window are counted as delivered. That second half is the one clients resist, and it is the one that stops response-time decay being billed back to the agency as a quality failure. The framing we use for the internal equivalent is in MQL versus SQL lead qualification.

Set the accuracy bar as a percentage you will actually inspect, not an aspiration. Ten records sampled at random each month, checked field by field against the specification, is enough to hold the bar honestly and cheap enough that it survives a busy quarter. Review the rejection reason list monthly and treat a reason that dominates as a specification bug rather than an agency failure. If forty percent of rejections are wrong company size, the enrichment source is misaligned and no amount of agency effort fixes it.

Auditing Lead Quality: Agency Records Against Your Response Times

Opinions do not settle this, evidence does, and fifty records is enough. Pull the last fifty rejected leads and for each one record four things: whether the firmographic fields actually match the ICP specification, whether the full payload arrived, the hours from handover to first logged human touch, and the rejection reason as given.

Then sort into four buckets. Specification mismatch, where the record genuinely fails the written ICP, is the agency's to fix. Payload incomplete is also the agency's. Touched late, where first contact fell outside the response window, is yours, and in our experience this bucket is consistently larger than clients expect. Readiness, not fit, where the record matches the ICP but the prospect is not in market, is a contract problem: you bought something the agency cannot supply.

The bucket distribution ends the argument because it is countable. Most audits we have run come back with the late-touch and readiness buckets together accounting for more than half, which reframes the conversation from the agency's performance to the design of the arrangement. Build the fit side of it properly and you need this audit less often, which is what win rate calibrated ICP scoring is for.

When the Agency Is Right and Sales Is Wrong

Sometimes the leads are fine. Three patterns recur. Reps reject records that need two or three touches because the comp plan rewards speed to opportunity, so a lead requiring work is rationally skipped. Reps reject accounts they have called before without checking whether the previous attempt was a different buying group or a different year. And reps reject anything that does not arrive pre-sold, which is a standard no agency can meet.

There is a structural reason to expect this. Gartner's research on the B2B buying journey reports that buyers spend roughly 17 percent of their total purchase time meeting with potential suppliers, and describes the journey as a nonlinear loop rather than a funnel. A lead reaching you mid-loop will look unready by any pre-sold standard while being entirely real. Rejection volume that correlates with rep rather than with record is the tell: when one rep rejects at triple another's rate on comparable records, the variable is the rep.

The reason this section exists is credibility. If your audit only ever produces findings against the agency, the agency stops treating the audit as evidence and starts treating it as a negotiation, and you lose the one mechanism that was working. The underlying argument about why the shared unit of account breaks is in why MQLs are dead.

Fix Your Agency Lead Quality With DevCommX

Run the fifty lead audit before your next vendor review, because the bucket distribution will decide that meeting either way and you would rather know the numbers first. If the late-touch and readiness buckets together come to more than half, the agency is not your problem and replacing them will cost you a quarter to learn that. What we build is the layer the audit depends on: the field-level ICP specification, the enrichment source of truth, suppression against open opportunities, the handover payload written straight into the CRM, and timestamps on first human touch so decay stops being arguable. That is revenue operations work and it stays with your team when we leave. Send us your rejection reason list and we will tell you which of the four buckets your problem is actually in.

Further Reading

  • Forrester, The Revenue Process Alignment Series Part 1: The End Of MQLs
  • Harvard Business Review, The Short Life of Online Sales Leads
  • Gartner, The B2B Buying Journey

References

  • Forrester, The End Of MQLs, source for the finding that inquiry to closed won conversion in a lead centric process typically runs under 1 percent
  • Oldroyd, McElheran and Elkington, Harvard Business Review 2011, The Short Life of Online Sales Leads, source for the audit of 2,241 US companies, the nearly sevenfold qualification difference within an hour, and the 23 percent non response rate
  • Gartner, The B2B Buying Journey, source for buyers spending roughly 17 percent of total purchase time with potential suppliers and for the nonlinear buying loop model

FAQ

Why are agency leads bad, or at least rejected so often?

More often they are leads qualified against criteria that were never specified. The contract describes an ICP rather than naming the fields, permitted values and data source, so the agency fills the gap with its own reading. The second common cause is a contract that pays for qualified leads while conflating fit with readiness, which asks the agency for in-market timing signals it cannot observe from outside your systems.

How do you define a qualified lead with an agency?

Separate fit from readiness and specify fit in field-level terms: which firmographic fields, which permitted values, and which provider is the source of truth. Name the buying roles that count. Then state readiness separately and be explicit about whether the agency is responsible for it. A scoring threshold is not a definition, because nobody can audit a record against a number they cannot decompose.

What should an agency hand over with a lead?

Nine fields: company identifier, the specified firmographic fields with the provider named, the contact and their buying role, the stated problem in the prospect's own words, source and campaign, the consent record with timestamp and wording, what the prospect was told would happen next, the agency's one-sentence qualification note, and a handover timestamp. It should write to your CRM directly rather than arrive as a spreadsheet.

How do you tell whether lead quality, agency performance or your own follow-up is the problem?

Audit the last fifty rejected leads and sort them into four buckets: specification mismatch, incomplete payload, touched outside the response window, and matches the ICP but is not in market. The first two are the agency's. The third is yours. The fourth is a contract design problem. The distribution is countable, which is what ends the argument.

What should a lead qualification SLA contain?

A two way commitment with a consequence clause. The agency commits to the field-level specification, the full handover payload and a stated accuracy bar. You commit to a response window, a rejection window, and a structured rejection reason from a fixed list. Then name the consequence both ways: out-of-specification records are replaced, and records not touched inside the window count as delivered.

Can sales be wrong about agency lead quality?

Yes, and checking for it protects the audit's credibility. Watch for rejection rates that vary more by rep than by record, reps skipping leads that need several touches because the comp plan rewards speed to opportunity, and accounts rejected as already contacted without checking whether the earlier attempt involved a different buying group or year. If every finding goes against the agency, the audit stops being treated as evidence.
